https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Christopher Phillips pleaded guilty to preventing a decent and lawful burial and two counts of fraud. Photograph: South Wales police/PA View image in fullscreen Christopher Phillips pleaded guilty to preventing a decent and lawful burial and two counts of fraud. Photograph: South Wales police/PA Crime Man jailed for keeping dead mother’s body in freezer and pocketing her benefits Christopher Phillips, who had been his mother Sylvia’s primary carer since 2008, given two years and four months in prison Steven Morris Mon 3 Aug 2026 08.38 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 09.49 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A man has been jailed for keeping his dead mother’s body in a freezer at their shared home for almost three years, during which time he received more than £70,000 of her benefits and other funds. Christopher Phillips, 60, stored the body of Sylvia Phillips, a retired company secretary, in the chest freezer in the living room of their house in the south Wales seaside town of Porthcawl. He regularly placed flowers on top of the freezer, which he bought two days after her death, and carried on talking to her about soap operas and horse racing. When police arrived to check on his mother, who was 89 when she died, he told them she was away in London, but they found her body after spotting flowers on the freezer. Phillips, a former company director, accessed his mother’s bank account, made withdrawals from her savings and pocketed benefits, Merthyr crown court heard. Judge Tracey Lloyd-Clarke, the recorder of Cardiff, sentenced Phillips to two years and four months’ imprisonment. She told him: “You continued to collect her prescriptions and misled medical professionals about her whereabouts, lying when inquiries were made about your mother, repeatedly telling medical staff that she did not wish to attend appointments or undergo tests. “Your mother’s pension and benefits continued to be paid into her bank accounts, which you were able to access.” Ruth Smith, defending, said Phillips had been “exceptionally close” to his mother. The pair had lived together for 50 years of his life and Phillips had been the primary carer for his mother since 2008. Smith said the defendant had told police: “I basically didn’t want to let her go.” She added: “He described talking to her as if she was still alive … sitting next to her, talking to her about television programmes, Coronation Street, the horse racing, just as they always did. “Mr Phillips was a vulnerable individual with a vulnerable mental health situation at the time of his mother’s death.” The court heard Phillips had left work to become a full-time carer in the months leading up to her death in March 2023. He was caught after police carried a welfare check because doctors had raised concerns they had not heard from his mother. When officers attended the house in February this year, Phillips said his mother was in London with cousins. Officers pressed further but Phillips would not give the details of which cousins or where they lived. His mother’s body was found covered with a leopard print throw and alongside it were roses and a birthday card reading “To Mum, from Christopher and Tina” – the latter being the family dog. Phillips pleaded guilty to preventing a decent and lawful burial and two counts of fraud. He received a total of £78,190.92 in state pension, pensions credit, attendance allowance, winter fuel payments, cost of living payments and housing benefit payments that would have ceased had his mother’s death been reported. The senior investigating officer, DCI Claire Lamerton, said: “This is an extremely sad case where Phillips concealed his own mother’s death and financially profited for a significant period. “My thoughts are with Sylvia’s loved ones during such a difficult time, and I hope they have found some peace having been able to properly lay her to rest.” Explore more on these topics Crime Wales news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

Financial Markets Authority chief executive Samantha Barrass is on leave, as workplace culture concerns are investigated. Photo / Dean Purcell An external party is being helicoptered into the Financial Markets Authority, as concerns over workplace culture issues have seen its chief executive take leave and a board member temporarily fill the role. A spokesperson for the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) says it is “engaging with the FMA board on appropriate next steps”. MBIE is getting involved, as it is the agency tasked with monitoring the FMA, the country’s financial markets regulator. The Chief Victim Adviser to Government, Ruth Money, told the Herald " multiple" past and present FMA staff raised concerns about the workplace with her. She escalated the matter accordingly. The Herald understands these concerns reached the Public Service Commission and Commerce and Consumer Affairs Minister last Friday. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. Soon after, on Wednesday, FMA chief executive Samantha Barrass went on leave and board member Alastair Hercus was made interim chief executive. The FMA issued a statement saying: “The FMA board has recently become aware of cultural concerns at the FMA and is assessing the matters raised as a matter of urgency.” For some time, word on the street has been that the FMA’s workplace culture has been poor, if not toxic. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. Various sources have spoken to the Herald about bullying behaviour involving staff at the most senior levels. The accounts align with those detailed in a Stuff article published on Wednesday. The FMA is understood to have relied heavily on keeping disgruntled staff quiet by getting them to sign non-disclosure agreements. Conduct regulator accused of poor conduct Issues bubbled to the surface in December, when the FMA’s chairman, Craig Stobo, temporarily stepped down, pending the outcome of a King’s Counsel (KC) review into his conduct. The review was initiated after three board members complained about Stobo to the minister. Stobo ended up resigning in May, after Wendy Aldred, KC, concluded he voiced too many political opinions for someone in an apolitical public sector role. Aldred’s report showed Barrass and the FMA’s general counsel and executive director for evaluation and oversight, Liam Mason, raised concerns about Stobo meeting with various organisations in Estonia (which is known for being very digitally advanced) with a former FMA employee, Kyla Bottriell. Aldred conceded there were “shortcomings” in Stobo’s communications with the FMA about the self-funded trip, but clarified there was no evidence of Stobo and Bottriell being in an inappropriate relationship, despite such rumours circulating. After Aldred released her report, Bottriell issued a statement saying: “The report corrects the public record, but it does not repair the harm, or answer wider questions about how a conduct regulator allowed misinformation to escalate, causing lasting damage to my reputation. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. “I have raised legitimate concerns through proper channels about the FMA’s internal culture, rumour-spreading, lack of accountability and leaking of internal matters. Those concerns predate this investigation and remain unaddressed. “The FMA holds market participants to standards of fairness, transparency and good conduct. It should apply the same standards internally.” Shortly after Stobo resigned, the FMA announced Barrass wouldn’t seek reappointment once her first term in the role ends in January. Barrass left one of her former roles, as Gibraltar Financial Services Commission chief executive, in 2019, nearly a year before her contract was due to end. She was involved in litigation during this time. Mediocre views of FMA According to an internal FMA survey done in September and October 2025, 59% of respondents saw a future for themselves at the FMA, despite 80% believing the work they did mattered and 72% feeling proud of their work. Of those surveyed, 61% said they would recommend the FMA as a place to work. These results were poorer than those from a survey done in February 2025. An FMA HR adviser attributed the deterioration to the impact of a recent organisational restructure and the reintroduction of a “performance framework”. She acknowledged “not all individuals are comfortable in a high-performance environment”. In 2025, the FMA also surveyed its stakeholders, including those it regulates. Just over half (56%) agreed it was easy doing business with the FMA – a slight improvement from the previous year. Meanwhile, 73% agreed the FMA was focused on the outcomes that mattered for consumers and 55% agreed the FMA’s approach to regulation was beneficial and proportionate. Commerce and Consumer Affairs Minister Cameron Brewer responded to the latest concerns raised around the workplace culture, saying: “It is important to me that New Zealanders are able to trust our financial and regulatory institutions. That is why any concerns that are raised must be properly considered and addressed. “I expect MBIE and the FMA to keep me informed on the outcomes of this process.” Jenée Tibshraeny is the Herald’s Wellington business editor, based in the parliamentary press gallery. She specialises in government and Reserve Bank policymaking, economics and banking . https://www.lynnnews.co.uk/news/male-who.text: Home News Article King’s Lynn man Donatas Sakalauskas sentenced for stealing from shops but will appear back in court for outraging public decency By Molly Nicholas - Molly.Nicholas@iliffepublishing.co.uk Published: 06:00, 16 August 2026 A thief who pulled the trousers down of a homeless man before having his penis touched will appear back in court. Donatas Sakalauskas, of Sir Lewis Street, Lynn, appeared at the town court on Thursday, pleading guilty to an act of outraging public decency along with five theft offences and a criminal damage charge. The court heard that on May 18 at the Cathedral Square in Peterborough, he approached a homeless man whom he did not know and bought him alcohol just before 11.30am. Magistrates Court house on College Lane in King's Lynn Sakalauskas pulled the victim's trousers down before exposing the male's buttocks and inserting his hand into his genital area and buttocks. The 42-year-old then kissed the victim on the lips, who then touched his penis. Prosecutor Lilika Peutherer said the incident was witnessed by members of the public. Magistrates sent this matter to Norwich Crown Court for Sakalauskas to be sentenced due to him already having an offence of a similar nature being dealt with. He was released on unconditional bail. However, the theft and criminal damage charge was dealt with during his court appearance. The bench heard that at 7.30pm on May 6, he entered the Tesco store at Hardwick, before exiting the shop with alcohol and various items to the value of £28.75. Then, within the space of an hour, the defendant returned and approached the security guard asking to buy a bag. The following day, Sakalauskas entered the same store, where he filled a trolley with items worth £45.25, before wheeling it through the doors, without making payment – he was seen outside the shop eating the stolen food. Three to four hours later, the man was detained by the security guard, who knew he was a “consistent shoplifter”, after re-entering the premises and stealing £69.45 worth of items. Over the two days, £140 worth of items are thought to have been stolen – some goods were retrieved while others were not. Sakalauskas has more than 30 charges in relation to theft offences. Furthermore, on May 24, the defendant entered Sainsbury’s at the Vancouver Centre in Lynn, where he selected food and alcohol before leaving without paying for the items – the value is unknown. Then, on June 2, he attended Heron Food in the town centre where he stole a £1.49 energy drink. The court then heard that on May 21, the defendant caused damage inside Sainsbury’s at the Vancouver Centre when he selected three bottles of wine, while “highly intoxicated” and then dropped one of them on the floor – worth £5.25. His last criminal damage offence was in December of last year. In mitigation, duty solicitor Alison Muir said he has some problems. She said his family in Lithuania disowned him because of his sexual preference. The court also heard that he has a partner of three years and he started his job a few weeks ago working at a local chocolate factory. For the theft and criminal damage charges, he was fined £416 and was ordered to pay compensation of £140 to Tesco and £60 to Sainsbury’s. There was also a victim surcharge of £166 and court costs of £85. Courts Crime Molly Nicholas Read the Your Local Paper e-edition for free here MOST READ

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Australian Greens senator David Shoebridge, pictured, has compared Labor’s new migration plans with those of the Trump administration. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP View image in fullscreen Australian Greens senator David Shoebridge, pictured, has compared Labor’s new migration plans with those of the Trump administration. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP Australian politics Labor visa overstayer detention centre plan branded a ‘Donald Trump twist’ on immigration Australian Greens senator compares government’s policy to ICE as Tony Burke calls it a ‘ridiculous claim’ Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Caitlin Cassidy and Sarah Basford Canales Fri 18 Sep 2026 04.30 EDT First published on Fri 18 Sep 2026 03.40 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The federal government’s move to reopen detention centres for visa overstayers, overseen by compliance officers, has drawn comparison from the Greens and advocates to Donald Trump’s sweeping immigration crackdown in the United States. The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, was careful to downplay any similarities when he announced the federal government’s immigration plan on Thursday, which includes reducing the roughly 77,000 unlawful non-citizens in Australia. He told the National Press Club the policy was returning to a “routine process” that existed before 2015, whereby overstayers were brought into detention centres if their visas lapsed prior to securing flights home. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here “This is not the sort of operation that some people have seen on TV happening in other countries,” Burke said. Burke said 100 new compliance officers would be hired to round up overstayers, and an additional 250 beds would be freed, as well as potentially repurposing a 100-bed quarantine facility in Victoria. He said most people would be placed in detention for a matter of weeks, and encouraged to leave of their own accord. Greens immigration spokesperson, David Shoebridge, said Labor should make visa processes and appeals faster rather than focusing on net migration figures. “This is where Labor has sunk to, reheating Tony Abbott’s immigration attacks, with a 2026 Donald Trump twist,” he said. 1:23 Australia announces immigration changes, including new visa policy for foreign students – video “Labor’s new immigration jails will be run by the same exploitative US private prison multinational that is already abusing people’s rights in immigration detention here. “If the minister doesn’t want these policies to be compared to ICE, he should not behave like ICE.” In 2025, the US private prison company Management and Training Corporation won a $2.3bn contract to run onshore detention in Australia under its local subsidiary Secure Journeys, despite serious concerns about MTC’s track record. MTC is one of a handful of private prison operators running ICE detention facilities . Burke told Guardian Australia Shoebridge was making a “ridiculous claim” by comparing Labor’s policy to the Trump administration’s immigration stance. “The Green party knows it isn’t true,” he said. “We are simply going back to what Australia had done for decades until mandatory cancellation started, which was to have around 250 beds used when someone no longer had a visa but was refusing to leave.” The shift occurred under then immigration minister, Peter Dutton, who introduced mandatory visa cancellations for criminal offenders in 2014, which rapidly filled detention centres and saw the department quietly pivot to issuing short-term bridging visas for low-risk overstayers to manage voluntary departures. Ramping up removals forms part of Labor’s plan to bring net overseas migration down from 292,100 to meet budget forecasts of 245,000 in 2026-27 and 225,000 each year thereafter. The former head of the Australian Human Rights Commission, Dr Gillian Triggs, told AAP that Australia’s pre-2015 migration detention regime put children in a “horrific pipeline”, with hundreds held in detention without education, most of whom were “severely mentally and physically ill”. In 2023, a landmark high court decision outlawed indefinite detention without reasonable prospect of being returned to one’s own country, but it’s unclear how that might apply to this change. The CEO of the Asylum Seeker Resource Centre, Kon Karapanagiotidis, said the federal government had demonstrated “the right to seek asylum and the right to work while seeking safety remain in danger”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Politics, really Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you after newsletter promotion Backpacker ballot and detention centre for visa overstayers: what we know about Australia’s new migration plan Read more “Minister Burke went to great lengths to reassure Australians this would not look like Donald Trump’s immigration raids,” he said. “But look at what is actually being planned … This will double Australia’s immigration detention regime. “We will not stand by while migrants and refugees are used as political punching bags.” Abul Rizvi, a former deputy secretary of the immigration department, downplayed the ICE comparisons, pointing out that up until 2015, compliance officers wore “shirts and a tie”, not military gear and were unarmed. “They operated completely differently,” he said. “They did not enter any premises of any employer without the permission of the employer or a warrant.” Rizvi said one of the “biggest functions” of the compliance team was educating employers about how to check the working rights of foreign employees, which he said “all appears to have stopped”. “Given that this cohort is at record levels and grows by around 1,000 per month, what should the government do about a cohort with no remaining right to be in Australia, noting that this cohort will be highly vulnerable to exploitation and live in the shadows of society?” he said. The legal director at the Human Rights Law Centre, Sanmati Verma, said the federal government should invest in protection for undocumented migrants who had been exploited at work rather than “needlessly expanding the punitive immigration detention network”. “Rounding up undocumented migrants and locking them in detention is a profoundly anti-worker proposal that undermines the Albanese Government’s commitment to stamping out modern slavery,” she said. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/23/erdo.text: "A Europe that excludes Turkey from its security architecture cannot possibly be stronger or safer," Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan told the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, seeking a more central role for his country in European security as trans-Atlantic relations remain strained under the Trump administration."As an integral part of Europe, our country plays a significant role in ensuring the welfare and security of the European continent," he said, referencing the NATO summit Ankara hosted in July as a "concrete manifestation" of Turkey's commitment."We are shaping our future with the European Union precisely through this strategic vision, and we expect the same vision from the European Union as well."Erdoğan has repeated the same stance since at least April 2025, when he told the Antalya Diplomacy Forum that "It has become clear once again that European security is unthinkable without Turkey.""Turkey is ready to take responsibility for European security in the future as well," he said at the time.Europe's indispensable partnerNATO member Turkey has been positioning itself as an indispensable partner as the White House signals that Europe must take greater responsibility for its own security, including in Ukraine, where Russia's all-out war has continued well into its fifth year.As the leader of the vast Mediterranean country of some 88 million with NATO's second-largest military and a substantial domestic defence industry, Erdoğan has preserved relations with both Kyiv and Moscow throughout the war, serving as a Black Sea broker."First and foremost, we are compelled to change the current mindset where international law is applied differently to the strong versus to the weak," Erdoğan said in his speech."Secondly, whenever international efforts fall short in resolving crises, we must harness regional ownership as an effective means of addressing those issues," he added."As Turkey, whenever we have acted upon this principle, as in the case of the Black Sea Grain Corridor, we have achieved results, and we have contributed to both regional and global security."According to Erdoğan, cooperation and open diplomacy are at the core of the world's future."History has shown us time and again through bitter experiences that there is no winner in a political approach which is built on mistrust," he emphasised.In his speech at UN headquarters in New York, the Turkish president also discussed his relationship with his US counterpart Donald Trump."I believe that our relations with the United States will flourish in every field during President Trump's second term, also with the contribution of our close friendship with him," Erdoğan said.Turkey applied for European Union membership in 1987, but the accession process has been stalled since 2018.A European Parliament report last year said the process could not be relaunched in current circumstances despite Turkey's geopolitical importance, citing the arrest of Istanbul Mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu, the crackdown on protests and broader democratic backsliding.Reform the Security Council, Erdoğan saysOn the UN Security Council, Erdoğan called for fundamental reform, arguing the current structure was no longer fit for purpose."The United Nations, established 81 years ago to maintain peace and security, has become unable to fulfil this mission, or rather, it has been made unable to do so," he said."Let's recognise that a system in which the will of more than 190 countries is subject to the whims of five countries is neither fair nor capable of fully establishing trust."Erdoğan proposed abolishing the veto power held by the five permanent members — the US, Russia, China, the UK and France — and replacing the current structure with a council whose members the General Assembly elects for fixed terms, with no permanent seats."The Security Council must absolutely be reformed in accordance with the principle that the world is bigger than five," Erdoğan said.Towards the end of his speech, the Turkish president stated that his country will "not remain silent in the face of injustice, and we’ll never consent to oppression.""When we look at the course of the world today, we can see that there are two paths before us," he said."Either we’ll deepen uncertainty through fear, through conflict and isolation, or we’ll build the future together through justice, solidarity and common will.""Of course, it is easy to punch darkness, what is difficult is to light a candle that will dispel that darkness," Erdoğan said."Turkey has chosen the second path, and hopefully we’ll follow it with patience," he concluded.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6m2.text: Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images Image caption, Estonian company Milrem Robotics makes unmanned military vehicles such as this one By Paulin Kola Published 4 hours ago Russia was behind an arson attack on an Estonian defence company in the capital Tallinn last month, authorities say. Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the attack on Milrem Robotics - which supplies Ukraine with unmanned military vehicles - was ordered by Russian special services, but gave no details. Moscow has been accused of launching sabotage attacks in a number of Nato countries that have been helping Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its neighbour in February 2022. Russia denies such allegations and has been quick to reject the Estonian accusation, too. But EU countries have rushed to Estonia's support, adding such attacks will not deter them from helping Ukraine. The attack on Milrem Robotics occurred on the night of 14-15 August. Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said that, based on information collected by the country's Internal Security Service, "we can conclude with certainty that the arson attack... was an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation". Security service chief Margo Palloson told broadcaster ERR that Russia was "constantly planning, looking for opportunities, trying to find people who would carry out attacks", but that last month's arson attack was its first successful attack this year. The foreign minister said the perpetrators had been arrested and Palloson said they were Latvians who had been living in Russia and taken part in previous attacks. Three suspects were arrested in Latvia and extradited to Estonia earlier this month. Margus Tsahkna said that "this act of sabotage is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe, aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine". French President Emmanuel Macron responded to Estonia's assessment, saying "the multiplication of these hostile acts represents a dangerous escalation by Russia, which will only lead it into a dead end". He mentioned the incident at Leipzig airport in Germany in August, in which an explosive-laden drone was found near Ukrainian cargo planes. "Russia needs to know that it will not overcome our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine," Macron added. An EU spokesman said the 27-member bloc would not cease supporting Ukraine. Nato chief Mark Rutte urged European governments to stay calm and continue supporting Ukraine. "Russia continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies. It is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine. But Russia is failing. It is failing on the battlefield in Ukraine and it is failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine," Rutte said. Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage - and Russia is the chief suspect Published 4 September Germany says Russia behind Leipzig airport drone attack Published 2 September Inside the Russian explosives plot that sent incendiary parcels to the UK Published 11 March In August alone, Russia was either accused or suspected of the Leipzig airport attack in Germany, a major fire at a warehouse of a defence firm in Bulgaria, a large explosion at a munitions factory outside Rome in Italy, an attempted arson attack on a Ukrainian-owned drone manufacturer in Slovakia, and two suspicious fires in Poland - the latest in a country which has reported several such attacks. Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms that tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyber-attacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary. Estonia's internal security service, known as Kapo, said Russia was continuing to look for further opportunities for either sabotage or other hostile acts. "Individuals recruited for such operations may be misled or manipulated and may be given false or fabricated justifications for their actions in an effort to conceal the involvement of the Russian state," Kapo head Palloson said , external . Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary. On Tuesday, President Vladimir Putin's spokesman said "such statements are baseless, ill-considered, have absolutely no relation to reality, and lack any form of reasoning". "We cannot and will not take such statements seriously," Dmitry Peskov said. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/16/hung.text: Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar held his first bilateral meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on the sidelines of the European Council summit, following months of negotiations over when and where the two leaders would meet.The highly symbolic encounter marks a step towards normalising relations between Kyiv and Budapest after years of tension.Under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, Hungary portrayed Ukraine as a security threat, while Orbán fiercely opposed Kyiv's bid to join the EU.Following his Tisza Party's election victory, Magyar pledged a more pragmatic approach and sought to repair relations with Ukraine. However, his government has continued to insist that Kyiv fulfil its commitments on minority rights before further progress towards EU membership can be made.On Monday, Ukraine’s parliament approved the new legislation, which Zelenskyy subsequently signed into law. The following day, the EU opened negotiations on two additional accession clusters after Hungary dropped its objections, bringing the total to four out of six."As a first step towards restoring mutual trust, we assessed that the Parliament of Ukraine adopted the law on minority education based on the agreement, and that the Ukrainian side immediately began its implementation" Magyar said after the meeting in a social media statement.According to the Hungarian PM, further talks are expected between the two government on ministerial level."I assured the Ukrainian President of my full solidarity with the inhuman Russian aggression against her country that has been going on for almost five years" Magyar said.Zelenskyy also released a statement on social media, where he thanked the Hungarian PM for the solidarity with Ukraine and for the opening of two negotiating chapters in their EU accession process."We are working to open the remaining two by the end of the year. We discussed the diplomatic situation and efforts to end Russia's war. I am grateful for his solidarity with Ukraine and our people, and for his readiness to work together for peace," Zelenskyy said in a post released on X."Ukraine always stands for good-neighborly relations and mutual strengthening. We agreed to resume joint work at various levels and to exchange visits," the Ukrainian President added.Further meeting plannedMagyar and Zelenskyy are set to meet again soon. Magyar said a meeting could take place in the autumn in Berehove, western Ukraine, a centre of the country’s 100,000-strong Hungarian minority.Zelenskyy might also visit Budapest next week for the 70th anniversary commemoration of the 1956 revolution, a defining moment in Hungarian history. His deputy chief of staff, Ihor Zhovkva, confirmed in an exclusive interview with Euronews that the president had received an invitation and was considering the visit.“We have received an invitation. On 23 October, an event will be held to mark the 70th anniversary of the Hungarian Revolution,” Zhovkva said when asked whether Zelenskyy had been invited to the Hungarian capital. “The President of Ukraine has received an invitation to attend. We shall see.”On 23 October 1956, Hungarian students took to the streets to protest against Soviet occupation. The demonstrations quickly grew into a popular uprising, which the Red Army later crushed. A visit by Zelenskyy could also invite parallels with Ukraine’s defence against Russia’s full-scale invasion.
